I have been working this land for nearly fifty years. I know every mu of it. My body is older now but my knowledge is deep. Let me think through what I will do this year.

My main system is wheat and maize on the same land — wheat in autumn, maize after harvest in summer. That is the backbone. Five mu for that rotation. I keep this going every year because it is reliable and I know how to do it in my sleep. My son and daughter-in-law help during the busy periods, but otherwise I manage myself.

I will keep 2 mu of cotton. Cotton prices have been falling and it is hard work — picking is painful on the back at my age. But I have grown cotton for forty years and I know how to read the plants. I will not abandon it completely. The income supplements the grain.

One mu of mungbean on the remaining land. My family eats them and I sell a little. Not much input needed — mungbean fixes its own nitrogen somewhat, and I do not apply as much fertilizer. I save seeds from last year, which I have done for decades.

For wheat, I buy improved seed from the township seed station — same variety I have used for years, I know how it behaves here. I plough in October before sowing, apply base fertilizer, then top-dress nitrogen at jointing stage. Four irrigations: pre-sowing, wintering, jointing, heading. Two pesticide sprays — one herbicide early, one fungicide when I see risk of rust.

For maize, I buy hybrid seed — everyone does now, the hybrids yield much more. After wheat harvest I use the rotary tiller quickly to prepare the bed because timing is tight. Three irrigations. Two sprays.

For cotton I plough in spring, apply heavy base fertilizer, then top-dress multiple times. Cotton needs the most attention — five pesticide applications for bollworm and aphids. Four irrigations.

For mungbean — minimal input. I save my own seed, rotary till, two irrigations, one pesticide spray if I see serious pest pressure.
